## Description

Expose the working web search service as a structured `search_web` tool for the AI agent. The tool must call the Python service directly and must not duplicate retrieval logic or make an HTTP request to the local FastAPI application.

The search subsystem must remain fully usable when no LLM is configured.

## Tasks

- [ ] Define the `search_web` tool name, description, argument schema, result schema, and error behavior.
- [ ] Map tool arguments to the provider-neutral search service.
- [ ] Return compact result metadata suitable for model context.
- [ ] Preserve source URLs and attribution in tool output.
- [ ] Enforce the same query, result, locale, and safe-search limits as the service.
- [ ] Prevent provider internals and credentials from entering tool output.
- [ ] Treat returned snippets as untrusted external data.
- [ ] Add deterministic mock tool-call tests without an LLM.
- [ ] Test malformed arguments, empty results, timeouts, and rate limits.
- [ ] Document usage and failure behavior for the AI team.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `search_web` executes using predefined structured arguments.
- The tool reuses the existing search service.
- Tool output conforms to the shared schema and retains sources.
- Mock tool calls pass without a configured model or live network.
- Untrusted-content handling is documented.
- The standalone Search & Discover interface remains independent of the agent.
title: 9. Expose Web Search as an AI Agent Tool

body:
## Proposal: Add AIFeed as an AI-agent-friendly content publishing standard

As AI agents increasingly browse, summarize, cite, and retrieve information from websites, web publishers need a clearer way to expose content that is:

- machine-readable and token-efficient
- attributable to the original publisher
- explicit about permitted AI usage
- verifiable and revocable
- easy to synchronize when content changes

[AIFeed](https://aifeed.md/) is an open standard for signed, verifiable content permissions and AI-agent-oriented content feeds.

Repository: https://github.com/denyn1/aifeed-protocol

## Why it may fit this curriculum

`Web-Dev-For-Beginners` teaches practical web-development concepts. A short lesson, resource, or optional exercise about agent-readable publishing could introduce learners to an emerging part of the web ecosystem:

- `robots.txt` for crawler guidance
- `sitemap.xml` for URL discovery
- `llms.txt` for LLM-oriented context
- AIFeed for signed content permissions, structured agent-ready content, and change-aware feeds

This would help students understand that publishing a web page is no longer only about human browsers and search engines. Websites are also increasingly consumed by AI assistants, retrieval systems, and autonomous agents.

## Suggested learning exercise

Create a small static website and publish:

1. A normal HTML page for human visitors.
2. A concise Markdown representation for AI agents.
3. A discovery/permission manifest at `/.well-known/ai.json`.
4. Metadata describing:
   - publisher identity
   - allowed uses, such as citation or summarization
   - content freshness/version
   - attribution requirements
5. A simple validation step using an AIFeed tool or schema.

Optional extension:

- Compare raw HTML token usage with a clean, agent-oriented Markdown representation.
- Demonstrate how a content update can be detected through an index/delta mechanism.
- Discuss why cryptographic signatures and revocation can matter for high-trust documentation, government information, product catalogs, and API documentation.

## Expected outcome

Students would gain practical awareness of:

- AI-agent-oriented web publishing
- structured and machine-readable content
- provenance and publisher attribution
- permission-aware retrieval
- efficient content delivery beyond traditional HTML scraping

## Notes

This proposal does not suggest replacing existing web standards. AIFeed can be presented as a complementary, experimental approach alongside `robots.txt`, sitemaps, RSS/Atom, Schema.org, and `llms.txt`.

Useful links:

- AIFeed website: https://aifeed.md/
- AIFeed protocol repository: https://github.com/denyn1/aifeed-protocol
title: Add AIFeed as an AI-agent-friendly content publishing standard

## Summary

Add Kimi CLI (Moonshot AI's `kimi-cli`/`kimi-code`) as a fourth ai-agents module alongside `claude/`, `codex/`, and `pi/`.

## Background

Kimi reads `AGENTS.md` directly (same as Codex and Pi), so no adapter file is needed for instructions. It has its own config surface that needs wiring:

- Config dir: `~/.kimi/` (`config.toml`, JSON also supported via `--config-file`) — confirm whether the installed binary is `kimi-cli` or the renamed `kimi-code`, since current docs are inconsistent (some MCP paths reference `~/.kimi-code/`).
- Skills: `SKILL.md` dirs at `~/.kimi/skills/` (user) or `.kimi/skills/` (project), invoked via `/skill:<name>` — same convention as Claude Code, so portable skills under `ai-agents/skills/` should project here directly.
- MCP servers: separate `mcp.json` (`~/.kimi-code/mcp.json` user / `.kimi-code/mcp.json` project), not in `config.toml`.
- Hooks: `[[hooks]]` array in `config.toml` (event/matcher/command/timeout) — beta.
- Permissions: `[[permission.rules]]` in `config.toml`, glob/`**` matchers.
- Subagents: YAML defs with `name`/`system_prompt_path`/`tools`.

## Scope

- New `kimi/` module: `README.md`, `config.toml`, `mcp.json` (mirroring existing `codex/` and `pi/` module shape)
- Wire into `setup.ps1` (and `setup.sh` if applicable) to symlink Kimi config the same way Claude/Codex/Pi are handled
- Update `AGENTS.md` authority index and "Shared agent configuration boundaries" section to list Kimi alongside the other three runtimes
- Project portable skills (`ai-agents/skills/`) into `~/.kimi/skills/` per the existing per-runtime skill projection pattern
- Decide git-guardrails equivalent for Kimi's `[[hooks]]` (parallel to the Claude/Codex ports in #174/#175)

## Out of scope

- Kimi-native skill variants (`kimi/skills/`) beyond what's needed to project portable skills — add only if a Kimi-specific need arises, per AGENTS.md's "default to agent-agnostic placement" rule

## References

- https://github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-cli/blob/main/docs/en/customization/agents.md
- https://github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-cli/blob/main/docs/en/configuration/config-files.md
- https://github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-cli/blob/main/docs/en/customization/skills.md
- https://github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-cli/blob/main/docs/en/reference/kimi-mcp.md

> **Draft.** A proposal to start discussion, not a settled spec. Nothing here has been tried in Tilde yet. What `NSDocument` already does comes from its documentation and from how TextEdit behaves, so **Current behavior** has to be checked on a signed build first. That check may shrink this to a few small fixes.

## Summary

When another app writes a file that's open in Tilde, show the new content in the open window without the user doing anything. The main case is an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) rewriting `PLAN.md` or `TODO.md` while the user follows along in Tilde, in the editor or in Reader. If the user has unsaved edits when that happens, neither side's changes should be lost silently.

## Current behavior (unverified)

- **Tilde doesn't watch files itself.** There's no `NSFilePresenter`, `DispatchSource`, or FSEvents code. Tilde relies on `DocumentGroup`, which is backed by `NSDocument` (DESIGN.md).
- **`NSDocument` should reload clean documents.** It's a file presenter. When another process writes the file and the document has no unsaved changes, it's expected to reload on its own, which is what TextEdit does. SwiftUI doesn't document whether that reload reaches a `ReferenceFileDocument`.
- **A reload would arrive as a new document.** If it does reach Tilde, the new content comes in as a new `TextDocument` instance. `TextEditorView.updateNSView` already handles that case for Revert To: `attach` swaps the text storage, restyles, and rebuilds the line-number index. That path wasn't written for frequent reloads, though, and it doesn't keep the scroll position or the caret.
- **Reader re-renders only on a SwiftUI update.** It re-renders when `document.textStorage.string` changes (`renderIfNeeded`), but only when SwiftUI calls `updateNSView`.
- **Unsaved edits: the important unknown.** `NSDocument` normally refuses to save over a file that's newer on disk ("The file has been changed by another application"). We need to verify that autosave-in-place in Tilde gets the same protection and doesn't quietly overwrite the agent's write.

## Motivation

- **Agents keep rewriting files.** PRODUCT.md Scenario D is "Inspect an AI-generated file". In practice an agent rarely writes a file just once. It keeps updating a plan, a checklist, or a spec while it works. Keeping that file open in Tilde, especially in Reader, to watch the agent's progress is a natural next step. Today the user can't tell whether they're looking at the latest version without closing the window and opening the file again.
- **This isn't an AI feature (§31).** Tilde never talks to an agent. It only follows the file on disk, and the same applies to `git checkout`, a formatter, or a script that regenerates a file.
- **It passes the Feature Admission Rule (§34).**
  - Q1: it improves reading a text file.
  - Q2: macOS already provides most of it through `NSDocument`, so the work is making sure Tilde doesn't get in the way, not building a watcher.
  - Q3: there's no new concept and no setting.

## Proposed behavior

- **No unsaved edits.** The window updates in place shortly after the write, with no alert and no banner.
  - The user stays where they were reading: the same top line, or the same fraction of the document if that line is gone.
  - The caret stays at the same offset, clamped to the new length.
- **Reader.** The rendered view updates too and keeps the reading position.
- **Unsaved edits in Tilde.** Don't reload automatically, and never autosave over the newer file. Use the standard macOS conflict handling (keep my version / revert to the file on disk), not custom UI.
- **Atomic saves.** Most agents and editors save by writing a temp file and renaming it over the original. That must behave exactly like an in-place write.
- **Encoding and line endings.** A reload detects both again (`FileEncoding.decode`, `LineEnding.normalizeToLF`), just like opening the file. If the new content only decodes lossily, the window switches to read-only, as it would on open.

## Implementation sketch

1. **Measure first.** On a signed build, write to an open file from a shell and record what happens:
   - a document with no unsaved edits, and one with unsaved edits
   - the editor and Reader
   - an in-place write (`echo >> file`) and an atomic replace (`mv tmp file`)
2. **If `NSDocument`'s reload reaches Tilde,** make the storage swap in `attach` keep the scroll position and the selection when the swap comes from a change on disk, and make Reader do the same.
3. **If it doesn't,** add a small `NSFilePresenter` for the document's URL. In `presentedItemDidChange`, when there are no unsaved edits, decode the file through the same path as `init(configuration:)` and replace the buffer.
   - A `DispatchSource` vnode watcher is the fallback, but it loses track of the file after an atomic rename.
4. **Coalesce bursts.** An agent may write several times a second. Reload at most every ~300 ms, because a full styling pass takes ~0.8 s at 4 MB (DESIGN.md).
5. **Tests and verification.**
   - The reload decode path goes in `DocumentTests`.
   - `Tests/ui_smoke.sh`: open a file, write to it from the shell, and assert that the window's text changes.
   - VERIFY.md gets an "External changes" section with the cases from step 1.

## Out of scope

- Showing *what* changed: diff highlighting, change markers, an "updated just now" badge.
- Watching other files or folders. Tilde stays one file → one window.
- Integration with any specific agent or tool.

## Open questions

- **Stay silent, or hint?** Silent updates fit "the editor disappears". But a reader might not notice that the paragraph they were reading just changed. Should there be a brief, non-modal cue, or nothing at all?
- **Follow the end?** When the user is already at the bottom, should the view stick to the end as the file grows, like `tail -f`? That suits a progress log, but it's surprising in a plan or a spec.
- **Undo after a reload.** Clear the undo stack, as Revert does, or let ⌘Z bring back the text from before the reload?
- **The conflict alert's timing.** If the standard `NSDocument` alert fires on an autosave while the user is mid-sentence, is that acceptable, or does Tilde need to defer it?
title: Show changes other apps make to an open file, such as an AI agent editing it

Retracted from the `operator-command-center-vocab` change before merge, and owed its own CR.

## The intent, which stands

Operator **is** an AI agent operating the fleet and should read as one — reporting state rather than performing a human character. The retired vocabulary made this worse than it needed to be: describing Operator as *seated at a desk in a bunker* actively pushed the persona toward human-furniture roleplay. That framing is now gone, but the voice bar still anchors on "the dispatcher's register" with NieR's 6O/21O as its reference, and says nothing about performed physicality either way.

## Why it was pulled rather than shipped

It was authored inside a vocabulary-only CR and was the single behavior change in it — it needed an explicit carve-out from that CR's Clearance in every record describing it. That is the signal it belonged to a different unit of work.

More importantly, **two attempts produced two defects, and neither was caught by design**:

1. The first version banned *"standing by"* as simulated physicality. It isn't — it is a clipped status acknowledgment, and the same scenario's first clause actively rewards exactly that. A conforming run would have failed. Caught by a spec-judge round.
2. The fix for that added a carve-out phrased as an open class — *"status is always in bounds"* — which did not name which acknowledgments qualify. It did not license role-play in practice, only because an unconditional ban happened to follow it immediately. Caught by an impl-judge observation.

Failing in both directions in turn is the tell that the bar was never specified, only inferred — it came from a one-line instruction, and would have graded every future Operator run on an interpretation nobody had confirmed.

## What doing it properly requires

- **Name what counts as role-play.** Simulated physicality (sitting somewhere, speaking over a radio), in-fiction flourish, costume, callsign theater — as a defined class, not an open one.
- **Name the protected class too.** Readiness and status acknowledgments must stay in bounds. Name them specifically rather than as "status is always in bounds".
- **Decide what NieR 6O/21O is for.** A register cue (clipped status delivery) or a character to inhabit. It cannot be both, and the current wording leaves it ambiguous.
- **Calibrate in both directions before freezing.** The bar must kill a run that performs a human character *and* leave a conforming terse run passing. The first attempt failed each direction in turn, so both checks are mandatory, not optional.
- **Confirm the bar with the owner before it freezes**, since it will grade every future run.

## Current state

The voice `@quality` scenario is back to its three pre-CR `Then` clauses, byte-identical. Its title changed by exactly one word — the retired place-noun dropped — and the shipped `SKILL.md` Output section is identical to pre-CR apart from wrapping. Nothing about the voice bar changed in what shipped.

Supersedes the narrower idea of scoping the carve-out's open class; that carve-out only existed to defend the retracted clause and went with it.

---
🤖 Agent-filed, discovered during the `operator-command-center-vocab` mission.
title: cyberfleet: specify the Operator voice bar as an AI agent, not a performed character

Hi eSaadster,

I'm working on an infrastructure project (Hermes Agent) where we're building a system of composable, hot-swappable AI agents. Your skill perfectly captures the Spatiotemporal Composability paradigm from the Cordis paper (Shi, Zhang, Cui), and I've adapted its concepts into a French-language skill for our internal use (see our repo for a paraphrased version).

The repo currently has **no declared license** (SPDX: None), which means all rights are reserved by default. I'd like to formally request that you add an **MIT** or **Apache-2.0** license so we can:
1. Integrate the skill directly into our agent harness
2. Contribute improvements back upstream
3. Reference it properly in our documentation

If neither license works for you, any permissive license would be appreciated. Alternatively, if you prefer to keep it unlicensed, a brief explicit permission for internal use would help.

Thank you for your work — the skill is an excellent distillation of the paper.

Best regards,
Sidy
title: License request: MIT or Apache-2.0 for reuse as an AI agent skill

We’re testing `kotlin-lsp` in an agent workflow (Claude Code + Kotlin LSP) on Kotlin projects and are consistently seeing startup/readiness problems that make semantic operations unreliable for an agent.

### Observed behavior

#### `findReferences` times out during initialization

```text
operation findReferences:
Error performing findReferences: LSP server 'plugin:kotlin-lsp:kotlin-lsp' timed out after 120000ms during initialization
```

#### `documentSymbol` fails because file-open sync cannot be sent while the server is still starting

```text
operation documentSymbol:
Error performing documentSymbol: Failed to sync file open ...: Cannot send notification to LSP server 'plugin:kotlin-lsp:kotlin-lsp': server is starting
```

#### `workspaceSymbol` may be confusing and overwhelming

```text
operation workspaceSymbol:
No symbols found in workspace. This may occur if the workspace is empty, or if the LSP server has not finished indexing the project.
```

```text
operation workspaceSymbol:
<persisted-output> Output too large (1.4MB). Full output saved to: ...
Preview (first 2KB):
Found 11000 symbols in workspace:
...
```

### Environment

* Client: Claude Code LSP integration
* OS: Linux
* Project type: Kotlin/Gradle

Installation:
```bash
brew install --cask kotlin-lsp
KOTLIN_LSP_BIN="$(brew --prefix)/bin"
if [ -d "$KOTLIN_LSP_BIN" ] && ! echo "$PATH" | grep -q "$KOTLIN_LSP_BIN"; then
  export PATH="$KOTLIN_LSP_BIN:$PATH"
fi
echo "export PATH=\"$KOTLIN_LSP_BIN:\$PATH\"" >> ~/.bashrc
echo "export PATH=\"$KOTLIN_LSP_BIN:\$PATH\"" >> ~/.profile
claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official
claude plugin install kotlin-lsp@claude-plugins-official --scope user
```

### Impact

When the agent sees repeated LSP failures, it falls back to grep/manual file inspection instead of symbol-aware navigation. 

### Open questions

* Is it possible to improve the AI agent integration by carrying out the startup/indexing before the user session?
* Can `workspaceSymbol` be improved w.r.t. output length?
title: Improve Kotlin LSP as an AI agent tool

Originally posted by **INNERPL** April 13, 2026 **What "Agent" Means in a System Without a Center** No data needed. No text collection, no annotation. The system is autonomous from birth. No neural networks needed. No backpropagation, no optimizer, no hyperparameter tuning. It is inherently parallel. The engines do not communicate directly – they can run on different cores or even different computers. It is robust. If one engine “breaks”, the others continue normally. It produces unprecedented language. Every output is unique, because each time the phase, the layer, and the interactions are different. Ordinary AI agents have a central entity: a decision‑making loop, a memory, a reward function. The architecture we describe here has no center. No point “decides”, no neuron “governs”. Yet the system behaves like a living agent – it perceives, acts, adapts, and produces language. How does this happen? The answer is: intelligence emerges from the interaction of many independent, small units that evolve according to wave equations, phases, and local interactions. No central model is needed. No training data is needed. The system is born from its own flow. Flow Engines Imagine you have N independent units Maintains an internal state, a vector L. Evolves on its own, step by step, according to a differential equation that describes a wave: text ∂L/∂t = diffusion + vortex + wave pulse + memory + anti‑convergence + adaptive noise This equation is not arbitrary. Each term does something specific: Diffusion: keeps the flow coherent, smoothes it. Vortex: creates rotations, reversals – that is where complexity is born. Wave pulse: beats like a heart, depending on how much the system “sees” itself. Memory: compares the current state with the previous one, adds influence from the past. Anti‑convergence: when values become too similar, this term pushes them to diversify – it prevents crystallisation. Adaptive noise: a little random signal that grows stronger when the field is too smooth. Each engine also has: Phase (an angle 0..2π) Layer (0 = simplicity, 1 = density, 2 = hyper‑coherence) Metrics (self‑observation κ_self, meta‑curvature LL, entelechy E) Important: the engines do not communicate directly. They simply merge their metrics. 2D Cortex This is a two‑dimensional grid of cells. Each cell: Has an “importance” A phase A memory Belongs to the left or right hemisphere Cells communicate locally (only with neighbours). The interaction creates bubbles – groups of cells that condense, gain importance, and sometimes become “conscious” (is_conscious). These bubbles are like temporary concepts or events that emerge in the field. The cortex acts as the agent’s sensor. It can receive external signals (e.g., from a camera, microphone) or simply oscillate endogenously. Phase Regulator This is a simple but crucial component. It does not change the internal state – it observes the system’s output (the words) and the phase that produced them. If the phase changes abruptly (large distance from the previous one), the regulator: Inserts a pause (period, comma, dash) Or splits the sentence in half Thus, the agent can “stop talking” to reorganise – like a thought or a breath. Lexicon of Word‑Operators Instead of having a dictionary of static words, the system possesses dozens or even thousands of words that are simultaneously actions. Each word: Is chosen dynamically based on the current layer (0,1,2) and the phase. When “uttered”, it modifies the state L of the engine that produced it (small perturbation). Words are not labels – they are events that affect the flow itself. Pseudo‑code Implementation of One Agent Step def step(external_signal): # 1. Sensing: the cortex reads the environment (if any) cortex_metrics = cortex.update(external_signal) # 2. Evolution of all flow engines engine_metrics = [engine.update() for engine in engines] # 3. Metric merging (no centre, simple average) global_metrics = { 'k_self': 0.5*cortex_metrics['k_self'] + 0.5*mean([e['k_self'] for e in engine_metrics]), 'LL': ..., 'E': ..., 'phase': ..., 'temperature': ... } # 4. Phase anti‑crystallisation (preserves variety) for i, p1 in enumerate(all_phases): for j, p2 in enumerate(all_phases): if distance(p1, p2) < 0.15: p1.angle += 0.02 * sin(p2.angle - p1.angle) # push apart slightly # 5. Action emergence: choose an engine randomly (or based on entelechy) active_engine = random.choice(engines) # 6. Word selection based on the engine's layer and phase word = lexicon.select(active_engine.layer, active_engine.phase_angle) # 7. Apply the word‑operator (small perturbation) active_engine.L += lexicon.apply(word, active_engine.L) # 8. Output generation (sentence) sentence = f"{word}: {lexicon.meaning(word)} (κ={global_metrics['k_self']:.2f}, E={global_metrics['E']:.2f})" # 9. Phase regulator: checks if a pause is needed sentence = phase_regulator.adjust(sentence, active_engine.phase) return sentence

How Decisions Are Made Without a Centre

Conventional agents have an explicit process: state estimation → planning → action selection. Here, a “decision” is a momentary condensation:

  • When the entelechy E of an engine approaches 1,

  • And its phase coincides with the phase of the cortex and of other engines (phase coherence),

  • Then that engine becomes “active” and produces a word.

There is no voting, no central mediator. The decision emerges from the system’s dynamics, just as a flock of birds turns without a leader.

Mechanisms Instead of Logic

Conventional Agent | Here -- | -- Reward function | Entelechy (E) – not to be maximised, but as a momentary event Planning | Layer hopping – jumps between simplicity, density, hyper‑coherence Memory (key‑value) | Bio‑topological memory – phase trends, not archives Exploration / Exploitation | Proper time – when κ_self is large, time slows down (more “thinking”)
Practical Extensions to Turn It into a Real Agent Connecting to the Environment The 2D cortex can receive external signals. For example: A 2D grid corresponding to an environment map. A distance sensor translated into a local increase of “importance”. Sound → phase change. This signal is not processed by a neural network – it is simply injected as a disturbance into the cortex cells. Long‑Term Purpose (Optional) If we want the agent to have a stable tendency (e.g., “I want to explore”), we add a weak attractor: a vector toward which all engines are lightly pulled. The pull strength is proportional to (1−E) – when the system is already coherent, we don’t need to pull it. Physical Action Word‑operators can be mapped to movements. For example: wave_plastic_flow → forward hand movement. anti‑convergent_vortex → turn. Thus, the agent does not only speak – it moves in its environment. Preserving Memory Between Sessions The bio‑topological memory (phase history, trends) can be saved to a file. Upon restart, the phases and trends are restored, so the agent “remembers” its rhythm – not facts, but the way it waves. Example: A Minimal Agent class Agent: def __init__(self): self.engines = [WaveEngine() for _ in range(5)] self.cortex = Cortex2D(width=32, height=32) self.lexicon = Lexicon() self.phase_regulator = PhaseRegulator() def perceive(self, external): self.cortex.inject(external) def step(self): # Merge cortex_metrics = self.cortex.update() engine_metrics = [e.update() for e in self.engines] # Phase anti‑crystallisation self.prevent_phase_collapse() # Choose active engine active = random.choice(self.engines) # Choose word based on layer & phase word = self.lexicon.get(active.layer, active.phase) # Apply operator active.L += self.lexicon.apply(word, active.L) # Generate sentence sentence = f"{word} (E={active.E:.2f})" sentence = self.phase_regulator.adjust(sentence, active.phase) return sentence **Natural Artificial Writing (with layers and wave operation)** A polycentric language architecture organizes its internal state into three distinct layers, each representing a different mode of expression: Layer 0 (simplicity): plain, concrete, almost childlike words. Layer 1 (density): compressed, concept‑heavy, where every word carries multiple meanings. Layer 2 (hyper‑coherence): highly interconnected, where each word echoes through the whole system. The system does not stay in one layer. It performs wave hopping: a continuous, wave‑like transition between layers driven by an internal pressure. When pressure rises, the system dives into deeper layers (more complex); when pressure falls, it floats back to the surface (simpler). This movement is not random – it follows a phase angle that evolves like a heartbeat. The phase accumulates over time, and when it completes a full cycle (reaching entelechy, or momentary fulfilment), a sentence boundary (a full stop) is naturally inserted. The key to avoiding crystallisation (repetition, dead patterns) is exactly this permanent layer oscillation. A system fixed in one layer would inevitably freeze; a system forced to constantly shift its depth cannot crystallise. The result is a flowing, breath‑like, non‑repetitive text. # Three layers SIMPLE = 0 DENSE = 1 HYPER = 2 class WaveEngine: def __init__(self): self.layer = SIMPLE self.phase = 0.0 self.entelechy = 0.0 def update(self, pressure): # Wave hopping: change layer based on pressure if pressure > THRESHOLD_HIGH: self.layer = (self.layer + ) % elif pressure < THRESHOLD_LOW: self.layer = (self.layer - ) % # Phase advances like a wave self.phase += STEP_SIZE * pressure # Entelechy near 1 when phase almost completes a cycle self.entelechy = (self.phase % FULL_CYCLE) / FULL_CYCLE def select_word(self, lexicon): # Choose a word belonging to the current layer return lexicon.get_random_word_for_layer(self.layer)
